title: ESA's Hera Arrives at Asteroid Dimorphos to Nail Down the Key Deflection Ratio DART Could Not Measure
excerpt: ESA Hera mission has arrived at the Didymos-Dimorphos asteroid system to measure the momentum enhancement factor that explains why NASA’s DART impact deflected Dimorphos far better than predicted -- closing a critical gap in planetary defense planning that left mission designers unable to
content:
Four years ago, a spacecraft the size of a golf cart slammed into an asteroid at roughly 6.6 kilometers per second (about 14,760 mph) and shortened the moonlet's orbit by 33 minutes — 25 times better than the minimum threshold scientists had hoped for. It was arguably the most consequential physics experiment in human history, and it raised an uncomfortable question that nobody could immediately answer: why did it work so well?

This month, ESA's Hera spacecraft arrived at the Didymos-Dimorphos binary asteroid system to find out. The probe has entered what ESA calls its early characterization phase, flying hyperbolic arcs at 25 to 30 kilometers (15.5 to 18.6 miles) from Didymos's center and beginning the systematic survey that will, over the next several months, pin down the specific number planetary defense has been missing since DART's 2022 impact. That number is called β — and the gap in our knowledge of it is larger than most people realize.

DART Worked. We Just Don't Know Exactly Why.

When NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft struck Dimorphos on September 26, 2022, it did not simply push the moonlet like a billiard ball. The impact vaporized and excavated material, spraying a cone of ejecta — an estimated 730,000 kilograms (1.6 million lbs) of rock and debris — in roughly the opposite direction from the collision. That ejecta acted like rocket exhaust, adding momentum to the deflection far beyond what the spacecraft's own mass and velocity would have provided on their own.

The ratio of that total recoil momentum to DART's own incident momentum is β — the momentum enhancement factor. If β equals 1, the asteroid received exactly as much push as a pure billiard-ball hit would predict. If β is greater than 1, the ejecta rocket effect amplified the deflection. DART's measurement, published in Nature in 2023 by Andy Cheng and colleagues at Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, found β = 3.61 at Dimorphos's nominal estimated density — meaning the deflection was more than three-and-a-half times larger than a simple billiard-ball prediction would have given.

That sounds like great news, and it is. But here is the problem: the density of Dimorphos is not precisely known, and density is the dominant variable in the β calculation. Across the plausible density range — 1,500 to 3,300 kilograms per cubic meter — β ranges from 2.2 to 4.9. That is a factor-of-two uncertainty in the central variable for every future kinetic impactor mission.

What that means in practice: a planetary defense campaign sized using a β estimate of 2.2 would be wildly over-engineered if the true β turns out to be 4.9. Sized for β = 4.9, it would be catastrophically undersized in the other direction. For a scenario with years of warning and time to send multiple impactors, the uncertainty is manageable. For a last-resort scenario with limited lead time, it could mean the difference between success and failure.

Hera's primary scientific purpose is to eliminate that uncertainty. It will measure Dimorphos's mass precisely, derive its true bulk density, and reduce the uncertainty in β to roughly ±10 percent — from a planning margin of "somewhere between 2× and 5×" to something a mission designer can actually build to.

Why "Formation Flying" and Not Orbit

Hera's navigation around Didymos-Dimorphos requires a technique that sounds routine but represents a genuine engineering challenge. The spacecraft is not orbiting Dimorphos in the traditional sense — it cannot. The combined gravity of Didymos and Dimorphos at typical spacecraft approach distances is approximately 45,000 times weaker than Earth's surface gravity, far too weak to maintain a stable closed orbit at the velocities needed to traverse the tens of millions of kilometers to get there.

Instead, Hera flies what engineers call hyperbolic arcs: curved trajectories that bring the spacecraft close to the target, let it gather data, and then require a thruster firing every three to four days to prevent it from drifting away. At its current early characterization distance of 25 to 30 kilometers (15.5 to 18.6 miles), Hera moves at roughly 12 centimeters per second (about 4.7 inches per second) relative to the asteroid system — slower than a person walking, but precisely controlled.

The guidance, navigation, and control system was developed by GMV in Madrid, Spain. Because Hera is currently approximately 1.3 astronomical units from Earth — a signal round-trip of 10 to 15 minutes — real-time ground-commanded navigation is impractical during close-approach phases. The spacecraft uses autonomous optical navigation: an onboard computer processes camera images of Didymos and Dimorphos's surface landmarks, computes its position, and fires thrusters without waiting for human input.

Over the coming months, Hera will gradually reduce that formation-flying distance, eventually approaching to within roughly 5 kilometers (3.1 miles) of the asteroid system for detailed close-range mapping.

A Moon That Was Reshaped by the Hit

Before Hera can fully interpret what it sees, it needed a picture of Dimorphos before DART arrived. Radar observations from Earth and Hubble Space Telescope imaging had established a rough pre-impact shape. What those couldn't tell scientists was what DART actually did to the moonlet's internal structure.

A 2024 study by Sabina Raducan at the University of Bern, published in Nature Astronomy, provided the answer, and it was more dramatic than a simple crater. DART's impact redistributed approximately 8 percent of Dimorphos's total mass to new positions on and within the body, and ejected roughly 1 percent — an estimated 15 million kilograms (33 million lbs) — into interplanetary space. The asteroid's shape changed from an oblate spheroid (a slightly flattened ball) to a triaxial ellipsoid — elongated, like a watermelon. Dimorphos now librates: it rocks back and forth in its orbital orientation as it circles Didymos, the same behavior observed in tidally distorted moons.

That global deformation confirms that Dimorphos is a rubble pile — a loose aggregate of rocks, boulders, and regolith held together by gravity rather than by the material strength of a monolithic rock. Only a rubble pile responds to a collision at this scale with global restructuring rather than forming a contained impact crater. The ejecta that produced β = 3.61 came from a body that essentially shook apart and partially reassembled itself.

This matters for Hera's mission in a specific way. Hera's cameras will map Dimorphos to roughly 10-centimeter (4-inch) resolution — but it is not just mapping a crater. It is mapping a globally deformed body. The crater itself, the ejecta blanket, the internal porosity, and the libration dynamics all encode information about how the kinetic impact redistributed momentum through a rubble-pile body. Those data feed directly into the physics models that future planetary defense planners will use.

Dimorphos is approximately 151 meters (495 feet) across — slightly larger than the Leaning Tower of Pisa is tall. It orbits Didymos, its 780-meter (2,559-foot) parent asteroid, at a distance of roughly 1,200 meters (about 3,940 feet, or 0.75 miles).

Two CubeSats, Including the First Asteroid Interior Radar

Hera carries two shoebox-size CubeSats that will be deployed to conduct science the main spacecraft cannot perform from formation-flying distance.

Milani, named in memory of the mathematician who pioneered asteroid trajectory dynamics, will study the mineral composition and spectral properties of Dimorphos's surface using visible and near-infrared imaging. Its data will help characterize the material ejected during DART's impact and confirm whether Dimorphos's surface composition is consistent with Didymos having shed it through YORP-driven spin-up.

Juventas carries JuRa — the Juventas Radar — which is the first instrument ever designed and flown specifically to probe an asteroid's interior using radar. It operates at a carrier frequency of 60 megahertz, sweeping from 50 to 70 MHz, with a bandwidth of 20 MHz. Those frequencies correspond to wavelengths of roughly 5 meters in vacuum, allowing the instrument to penetrate up to approximately 100 meters (328 feet) into Dimorphos's rubble-pile interior, with a vertical resolution of 10 to 15 meters. The entire instrument weighs less than 1,300 grams (2.9 lbs).

JuRa's heritage is the CONSERT instrument flown on ESA's Rosetta mission, which became the first radar to probe a comet nucleus's interior when Philae landed on 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko in 2014. The engineering team includes EmTroniX, the University of Grenoble (UGA-IPAG), TU Dresden, Astronika, and Brno University of Technology.

What JuRa is looking for: internal layering and porosity variation that reveal how Dimorphos was assembled and how DART's impact propagated through its structure. If the radar detects large internal voids or distinct layers, those features constrain the formation scenario and validate — or invalidate — the rubble-pile impact models that produced the β = 3.61 measurement.

The Mission That Closes the Loop

Hera is the product of a €363 million program investment (approximately $407 million USD at current exchange rates) by ESA and its member states, built by OHB Bremen as prime contractor. It launched October 7, 2024, on a SpaceX Falcon 9 from Cape Canaveral, used an Earth gravity assist in December 2024 and a Mars flyby in early 2025, and arrived at the Didymos system this month after a journey of roughly 400 days.

The primary science phase runs through mid-2027. After that, ESA plans to repurpose Hera as a testbed for autonomous navigation technologies — the same guidance systems that future planetary defense missions, and potentially commercial and exploration spacecraft, will need to operate independently at small bodies.

Ian Carnelli, ESA's Hera project manager, described Hera's first year in space as "incredibly successful and action packed" before arrival at the target system.

The public can follow Hera's progress through ESA's Hera mission portal and the European Space Tracking (ESTRACK) network updates.

Frequently Asked Questions

What exactly is formation flying, and why can't Hera just orbit Dimorphos?

Orbital flight requires a gravitational field strong enough to curve a spacecraft's trajectory into a closed ellipse. The gravity at the surface of Dimorphos is roughly 0.0003 meters per second squared — about 45,000 times weaker than Earth's. At that level, any spacecraft approaching at the velocity needed to reach the asteroid from interplanetary space would simply fly past. Instead, Hera uses a series of precisely computed hyperbolic arcs — curved paths that come close to the target and then require active thruster firings every three to four days to maintain the desired relative position. It is closer to a boat holding station in a current than to a satellite in orbit.

Why does the β factor matter for future planetary defense?

β appears directly in the equation used to calculate how much deflection a kinetic impactor will produce for a given asteroid mass, composition, and impact geometry. If β = 3.6 ± 10%, mission designers can size a deflector with high confidence for a given threat scenario. If β is uncertain by a factor of 2×, they either over-design (wasting launch mass) or under-design (risking mission failure). The current uncertainty is too large for a confident single-mission response to a real threat.

Has any country announced plans for a follow-on planetary defense mission?

NASA's Near-Earth Object Surveyor telescope is designed to dramatically expand the catalog of known near-Earth objects below 140 meters — the size range that remains incompletely surveyed. The United States Space Force and NASA's Planetary Defense Coordination Office are developing updated deflection planning frameworks that will incorporate Hera's β measurement once published. No confirmed follow-on kinetic impactor mission has been announced as of publication date; the DART/Hera data will inform those decisions.

What happens if JuRa's radar finds something unexpected inside Dimorphos?

That is part of the point. If JuRa detects large internal voids, fractured layers, or a composition significantly different from the surface spectral data, it would require revising the physics models used to predict β for rubble-pile asteroids in general. That revision could affect how every future kinetic impactor mission is designed. Unexpected interior structure is not a failure — it is information that makes the next mission more reliable.

Can I follow Hera's progress in real time?

ESA publishes mission status updates and trajectory data through its Hera mission portal. The ESA Science & Technology team also publishes regular science updates and instrument status reports. Amateur astronomers with large aperture telescopes may be able to observe Didymos/Dimorphos photometrically from Earth during the mission period, though the system is currently approximately 1.3 AU distant.
